newsitem.title: TAIWAN: New Taiwan holiday sparks business complaints.
newsitem.headline: New Taiwan holiday sparks business complaints.

text.p: Taiwan's government created a new February 28 public holiday to try to atone for its darkest hour, the massacre by Chinese Nationalist troops of thousands of Taiwanese in a reign of terror on that date 50 years ago.

But in a liberalising Taiwan where democracy and capitalism hold sway, industrialists and officials complain the change was made without enough thought and say this symbolic healing of past wounds comes at the expense of today's economic productivity.

Top cabinet economic policymaker Chiang Pin-kung led the chorus of complaints, saying the government had acted rashly in agreeing to observe the "2-28" holiday this year, just three days after parliament approved its creation.
"The February 28 holiday was decided too hastily and it has too great an impact on Taiwan's industries," said Chiang, chairman of the Council for Economic Planning and Development.
"It will directly influence the nation's productivity. The economics ministry should plan to cut out some other holidays."

The new public holiday marks the day in 1947 when Nationalist troops, losing the Chinese civil war to the communists on the mainland, suppressed anti-Nationalist riots on the island killing an estimated 18,000 people.

Pressure from Chiang and industry prompted the cabinet to announce on Thursday that, while private business and government agencies were free to take Friday off, financial markets and the banking industry would remain open.
"Banking service and financial markets... have a big impact on both industrial enterprises and the common people," Vice President Lien Chan said following the cabinet decision.
"Taking a day off without prior warning would not be giving enterprises and people a reasonable notice," he said.
Taiwan opposition activists hailed the new holiday.

"Making 2-28 a national holiday has been a dream of Taiwan's people for the past 30 or 40 years," Shi Ming-teh, lawmaker and ex-chairman of the main opposition Democratic Progressive Party, told Reuters in an interview.
"The government has made a positive, accurate decision for its 21 million people," said Shih, who spent 25 years in prison for opposing the Nationalists' authoritarian rule.

Despite a political renaissance begun in the late 1980s, the ruling party did not begin to atone for the massacre until February 1995, when Lee Teng-hui, Taiwan's first native-born president, made the government's first official apology.
The following month, parliament approved granting up to T$6 million (US$218,000) to each survivor of known victims.

The Nationalist Republic of China of Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, who is widely blamed for ordering the massacre, took control of Taiwan after Tokyo's 50-year occupation of the island ended with Japan's World War Two defeat in 1945.

The massacre, sparked by an old woman's protest against expropriation of untaxed cigarettes, came as Nationalist troops moved to secure Taiwan in the face of their losing fight to fend off a communist takeover of the mainland.
Chiang's government fled into exile on the island after its final defeat by the communists in 1949.
